abstract: The rapid development of automotive industry results in a series of increasingly serious problems such as energy consumption and environmental pollution, so that developing the automotive steels with high-strength and low-density is of great significance for energy conservation and emission reduction. Recently, FeeMneCeAl system steel is favored by numerous researchers because of its low density and excellent combination of strength and ductility. However, too much Al addition inevitably triggers various changes of microstructure, deformation mechanism, and mechanical properties. In this paper, the composition design, production process, strengthening and strain hardening mechanism, and microstructure evolution are systematically expounded. The discussion mainly focuses on various strengthening (solid solution strengthening, grain refinement strengthening and precipitation strengthening) and strain hardening mechanisms (phase transformation-induced-plasticity (TRIP), twinning-induced-plasticity (TWIP), microbandinduced-plasticity (MBIP), shear-band-induced-plasticity (SIP) and dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR), etc.). Also, the existing problems and future challenges in FeeMneAleC low-density steels are pointed out via analyzing the service performance (cryogenic performance, impact toughness, fatigue performance, hydrogen embrittlement, wear performance, and tensile properties). Finally, we look forward to the future development direction of FeeMneAleC low-density steels and provide the valuable ideas. © 2023 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/). With the rapid development of automobile industry, fuel efficiency and greenhouse gas emissions become increasingly serious. More and more advanced high-strength steel or lightweight materials (such as magnesium alloy, aluminum alloy, and carbon fiber materials) are employed in automobile production towards the above issues via achieving lightweighting. However, their expensive material cost and poor service properties (formability, wear, and hydrogen embrittlement et al.) result in a limited application in automotive materials. Low-density steels, which are considered as the new generation automobile materials, have been developed to overcome the aforementioned shortages. As early as the 1930 s, Korter and Ton [1] first put forward the concept of FeeMneCeAl system steels with Ni and Cr additions in consideration of the development prospect of high-strength steels. To lower the cost and density together, Ham and Carin [2] adopted the cheap Al and Mn elements instead of expensive Ni and Cr elements to optimize the chemical composition of stainless steels in the 1958 s. In the 1980 s and 1990 s [3e5], the replacement of Ni and Cr in stainless steel was widely studied, whereas few scientific studies on lowdensity steels were reported. Until the 2000 s, Frommeyer et al. [6] systematically investigated the microstructure and mechanical properties of FeeMneAleC low-density steels and considered that this steel can be employed to equip automobile steels. Since then, FeeMneAleC low-density steels started to attract much attention.
